tip: To form an adverb, put yn before an adjective and it soft-mutates: da becomes dda. dawnsio'n dda = dances well.
yn before a verb-noun marks an ongoing action: mae e'n gweithio = he is working, literally he is at working.
Adjectives after a feminine noun soft-mutate: dewr becomes ddewr in ferch ddewr = brave girl.
Feminine nouns soft-mutate after the (y, yr, 'r): canolfan becomes ganolfan, as in mae'r ganolfan = the centre.
bron â means almost, and â aspirate-mutates the next verb: cyrraedd becomes chyrraedd.
The word o (of) soft-mutates the next noun: cymeriad becomes gymeriad. dipyn o gymeriad = quite a character.
Yes/no questions open with the verb form: Ydych chi'n gwerthu ...? = Do you sell ...?
Comparatives add -ach and take na for than: tlws becomes tlysach. dlysach na'r llun = prettier than the picture.
Pa (which) soft-mutates the following noun: diwrnod becomes ddiwrnod. Pa ddiwrnod = what day.
yn becomes ym and nasal-mutates the next word: pob becomes mhob. ym mhob man = everywhere.
Welsh splits know: adnabod for people, gwybod for facts. adnabod y dyn = know the man.
hen (old) comes before its noun and soft-mutates it: gwragedd becomes wragedd in hen wragedd = old women.
ellir is the impersonal can form and needs no subject: Ni ellir newid = one cannot change.
With ers (for), Welsh keeps the present tense to mean has been: mae hi'n byw ... ers = she has lived for.
For as ... as, use mor ... â; mor soft-mutates the adjective: caled becomes galed. mor galed â = as hard as.
tair is the feminine three, used with feminine nouns: tair ystafell = three rooms. Masculine takes tri.
Hoffwn i = I would like, and the next verb soft-mutates: dysgu becomes ddysgu. Hoffwn i ddysgu = I'd like to learn.
Welsh has no verb for have: Mae pen tost gen i = there is a sore head with me, so I have a headache. gen i = with me.
After fy (my), c nasal-mutates to ngh: car becomes nghar. fy nghar i = my car.
